transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-22 15:30 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Rajiv, Sara, Tom (CloudHarbor)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, good afternoon. Thanks for carving out time. quick intro — Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, Ethan our SE is with me. how's everything on your side?
[00:12] Rajiv Patel: Hey Maya, thanks. we're doing well. quick note, we are time-boxed today to 50 minutes because of the exec check-in after. I'm Rajiv, platform lead. Sara and Tom are here to cover networking and security.
[00:25] Ethan Park: Cool, quick agenda—helm packaging for the runtime-adapter, KMS flow for customer-managed keys, VPC egress/whitelisting, telemetry hooks, and then ops runbook and canary. We'll leave 10 minutes for Q's. Sound ok?
[00:37] Sara Gómez: That works. Our main constraint is no outbound to public internet from the namespace; everything has to go through our NAT/bastion and KMS must be customer-managed HSM.
[00:49] Tom Liu: Also we need audit logs to show key unwrap events for compliance, SOC2 stuff.
[00:55] Maya Chen: 100%. We'll show the KMS pattern we use — it's a two-step: model keys encrypted by customer KMS and then Redwood runtime receives wrapped key via the VPC-private API. Ethan, do you want to show the helm layout?
[01:08] Ethan Park: Yeah — i shared a quick slide deck, slide 4 has the chart layout. The chart is minimal: adapter image, deployment, configmap with model mappings, a secret mount for the wrapped key, and a sidecar for telemetry. Values.yaml has knobs for batch size, max-latency-ms, and quantization profile.
[01:28] Rajiv Patel: When you say "wrapped key" — just to be sure — the raw key never leaves our KMS, correct? We only pass an encrypted blob?
[01:36] Ethan Park: Correct. the raw DEK stays in your KMS, we request Decrypt on the KMS endpoint from the runtime's service account when spinning up the pod, wrapped material flows through the private API endpoint. If you need, we can support an audit callback so your KMS logs an explicit request ID.
[01:54] Tom Liu: That sounds ok. What about offline/onprem usage? We want to be sure the adapter can run air-gapped with an on-prem KMS.
[02:01] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports air-gapped deployments — there are a couple of ops differences. For marketplace listing we'd surface two variants: hosted onboarding (calls to Redwood control plane) and private mode which is the customer-managed runtime. For private mode we provide an operator and an offline packaging bundle — Ethan, there's a note about tarball packaging in the doc.
[02:21] Ethan Park: Right. For on-prem the helm chart has a flag 'privateMode: true' which disables outbound control-plane checks and relies on a local operator for model artifacts and metrics sink. We'll attach the local metrics adapter config.
[02:36] Sara Gómez: Metrics sink — do you support prometheus remote write or only push to Redwood?
[02:42] Ethan Park: Both. We recommend remote_write to your existing Prometheus to keep telemetry inside your VPC; alternatively we can ship encrypted metrics to Redwood observability with customer consent.
[02:56] Rajiv Patel: Ok good. Let's talk about network egress — our security team won't allow direct egress except to specific Redwood IPs via a NAT. Do you publish a fixed IP list?
[03:06] Maya Chen: We publish a stable egress IP range per region for Dedicated and Hosted. For Private/on-prem you control egress. We'll provide the IPs in the security pack in the follow-up.
[03:18] Tom Liu: Please make sure those are CIDR ranges, and we need a plan B if IPs change.
[03:24] Ethan Park: We'll include an ASN and a small change window. For the canary, we can also do a proxy inside your VPC so you pin one outbound appliance.
[03:35] Rajiv Patel: Good. Next—latency/quantization. Our product needs sub-200ms 99th percentile for short prompts (<=128 tokens). Any data on expected bump when applying int8 quant vs fp16?
[03:47] Ethan Park: Quant gives a 2x cost reduction typically, but latency varies. For short prompts, int8 can be slightly faster—kernels are optimized—but there's jitter. Our guidance: for sub-200ms SLOs stick with the small-batched FP16 path and enable prefix caching. For cost-sensitive workloads consider int8 with aggressive caching and smaller batch sizes. We'll attach benchmark artifacts.
[04:13] Sara Gómez: Prefix caching — do you need sticky sessions to preserve KV cache?
[04:18] Ethan Park: You don't need full stickiness; the runtime supports K-V cache hot-spot routing. But when you have long conversations and many keys, you may want session affinity per pod for best p99. We'll describe routing policies in the runbook.
[04:33] Rajiv Patel: Are there any special kube privileges the chart needs? We want to avoid cluster-admin.
[04:38] Ethan Park: No cluster-admin required. The helm chart uses a service account with a restricted RBAC role for Secrets get/list, ConfigMap get/list, and CRD permissions if you opt-in to the operator. We'll include the exact manifest.
[04:52] Tom Liu: We need to validate that RBAC before install.
[04:56] Maya Chen: We'll send an install checklist.
[05:00] [Slides shared: runtime-adapter-helm-v1.2.pdf]
[05:08] Rajiv Patel: About marketplace listing metadata — does Redwood need our billing hooks or do we register as a passive connector?
[05:15] Maya Chen: For the joint listing model, you register the connector metadata in the marketplace, which includes pricing tiers and billing webhook URL. The webhook can be in your control; Redwood will call it for metered usages. For private deployments billing can be outside marketplace.
[05:30] Sara Gómez: Can we set a minimum tier that prevents very small noisy calls?
[05:34] Ethan Park: Yes, you can set granularity and minimum billing unit in the listing metadata. We'll add an example.
[05:44] Rajiv Patel: Security: Tom needs to confirm KMS policy interactions. Tom, any immediate red flags?
[05:50] Tom Liu: Two things — we need to log decrypt requests with principal info, and we need the option to rotate keys without downtime. Is rotation supported?
[05:58] Ethan Park: Key rotation is supported. We provide a rolling reload hook that fetches a new wrapped key and restarts the pod or reloads the secret depending on your in-cluster secret mechanism. We can do zero-downtime with dual-key provisioning pattern. We'll include a sample rotation script.
[06:17] Rajiv Patel: Sounds good. Now runbook for canary — what should we expect?
[06:22] Ethan Park: Our recommended canary: start with 5% traffic to adapter version N in a dedicated namespace, run synthetic workloads for 24-48 hours capturing p50/p95/p99, token cost, and failure modes. If metrics pass, canary to 25% for another 48h, then 100% with automatic rollback if p99 > threshold. We'll share the canary playbook.
[06:43] Maya Chen: We'll also add an automated fallback policy for model variant fallback in case of capacity issues — i.e., route to a cheaper compatible model.
[06:51] Rajiv Patel: Ok. Can you clarify how much logging telemetry goes out by default? We want to avoid PII leaking.
[06:59] Ethan Park: By default we redact inputs flagged as PII, but you must also provide a local PII filter stage in the adapter. We recommend client-side token filters and server-side redaction. We'll include the default redact list and how to extend it.
[07:17] Sara Gómez: Perfect. About the helm chart — can you walk through values we should tweak for small clusters?
[07:22] Ethan Park: Sure — key values: replicaCount (default 2), resources.requests/cpus and memory, batch.maxTokens, batch.maxLatencyMs, quant.profile (none, int8, fp16), cache.prefixSize. For small clusters we suggest replicaCount 1 and very conservative resources plus aggressive caching to avoid spikes.
[07:44] Rajiv Patel: What about autoscaling? HPA or custom scaler?
[07:48] Ethan Park: HPA works with custom metrics from the sidecar (qps or token throughput). We also have a recommended KEDA scaler pattern for bursty traffic. We'll provide example manifests.
[08:01] Tom Liu: On metrics permissions — we need to keep metrics inside our cluster. Confirm the chart can be configured to disable remote forwarding.
[08:08] Ethan Park: Yes, set telemetry.forwardToRedwood: false and configure remote_write to your Prometheus.
[08:15] Maya Chen: Rajiv, you mentioned earlier you have a billing webhook requirement — was that a must or nice-to-have?
[08:21] Rajiv Patel: Nice-to-have for now, must-have for later. For the pilot we'll just log usage locally.
[08:27] Ethan Park: Understood. We'll default to local usage capture.
[08:31] [09:00 slide — canary-runbook.md link posted]
[08:55] Sara Gómez: Quick Q on model artifacts — how large are they and do you stream parts or do they pull whole model to disk?
[09:02] Ethan Park: Models are pulled to local disk at startup; we support sharded downloads for big models and streamed weights for supported formats. For the adapter we use a sidecar that fetches model shards and validates checksums. We'll include a sample S3 presigned URL flow for the download.
[09:18] Rajiv Patel: What's worst-case disk footprint for a 30B model?
[09:22] Ethan Park: For a 30B fp16 model, on disk around 120GB; int8 quant can cut that roughly in half depending on format. We'll include exact numbers in the attachment.
[09:36] Tom Liu: Ok. I want to flag compliance — we need encryption at rest and KMS integration. Is the model artifact in S3 encrypted with our KMS?
[09:44] Ethan Park: Yes, the presigned URL flow works with S3 SSE-KMS. The runtime validates KMS decrypt on download time.
[09:50] Maya Chen: We're going to attach the security pack after this meeting with the SOC2 summary and our KMS flow doc.
[09:58] Rajiv Patel: Helpful. Let's get into action timeline — can you deliver those artifacts this week?
[10:03] Maya Chen: We'll push the helm chart and README by 2026-09-24 and the security pack by 2026-09-23.
[10:09] Sara Gómez: Sounds good. A couple of smaller items — do you have an example values file tuned for GKE autopilot?
[10:16] Ethan Park: Yes, we have gke-autopilot-values.yaml. We'll include it.
[10:21] Rajiv Patel: Awesome. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[10:25] Ethan Park: Nothing major. We'll need the test namespace and kube credentials from you.
[10:29] Rajiv Patel: We'll provide a temporary read-only service account credentials.
[10:33] Tom Liu: One more security question — do you support KMS envelope encryption with a double-wrap for extra separation?
[10:41] Ethan Park: We do — it's part of the advanced KMS pattern. Our operator can accept an externally-wrapped key and perform an additional wrap inside the cluster. We'll document how to configure.
[10:53] Maya Chen: Great. We're about 12 minutes left. Anything else high priority?
[10:58] Sara Gómez: Could you confirm rollback behavior if canary fails? Immediate rollback or pause and manual?
[11:04] Ethan Park: Configurable. Default is automatic rollback to previous stable version if p99 breaches threshold more than N times in M minutes. You can opt for manual gate if you prefer.
[11:16] Rajiv Patel: We'll start with manual gating.
[11:19] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll set the default canary to manual for the pilot.
[11:23] [11:30 slide — runbook checklist screenshot]
[11:32] Tom Liu: For the audit logs, any way to integrate with our SIEM?
[11:36] Ethan Park: Yes, we support syslog/syslog-ng and fluentd for forwarding audit events. We'll provide mapping to common SIEM fields.
[11:46] Rajiv Patel: Perfect. We're good to proceed. Let's recap next steps.
[11:50] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood sends helm chart + values + gke/autopilot example, security pack including SOC2 summary and KMS patterns, canary runbook. CloudHarbor provides read-only kube creds, test namespace, list of egress IPs allowed, and point of contact for KMS policy. Then we schedule the canary week of 10/12.
[12:10] Sara Gómez: I'll coordinate creds and namespace by 9/29.
[12:16] Tom Liu: I'll send the KMS policy contact and allowed CIDRs by 10/01.
[12:21] Ethan Park: We'll upload the helm chart bundle to the shared repo and drop a link in the follow-up.
[12:27] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. I'll send minutes and the artifact links shortly.
[12:32] Rajiv Patel: Thanks team, bye.
